audit.reasoning: The coding (fixed-dominant, final; strict=false, dom=true) is correct but rested on a Wikipedia sentence with no held file and a probably-wrong page locator (Blust 1999:324; the stress passage is p.332 per two independent citing works). This audit fetched sources three open primary/instrumental sources into Li & Tsuchida 2001 Pazih Dictionary p.3 'Stress always falls on the final syllable.' (verbatim, scanned of PDF p.15) confirms; Macaulay 2020 (AFLA 26 proceedings, new-speaker instrumental data) confirms obligatory IP-final stress and refines with additional non-secondary stress on long-vowel /ai/ /au/ syllables and an IP (not word) domain; Lin 2025 shows the Kaxabu dialect defaults to final stress (98% of disyllables, 64% of trisyllables) with initial heavy syllables, PV/imperative affixation and compounding pulling stress leftward in longer wor

sources.quote: Stress falls on the ultimate syllable.

sources.citation: Lin, Chih-Kai. 2025. Metrical Stress in Kaxabu Revisited: A Corpus-Based Approach. In E. Dal Corso & E. Ragagnin (eds.), Time in East Asian Endangered Languages (Eurasiatica 22), 247-266. Venice: Edizioni Ca' Foscari. DOI 10.30687/978-88-6969-913-9/010 (open access).
sources.quote: "Blust (1999, 332), Lin (2000, 55), Li, Tsuchida (2001, 3), and Lu (2003, 41) have suggested that Pazeh exhibits final stress in citation forms." Kaxabu corpus (3,000+ entries): "In disyllabic words, final stress is prominent (98%, 923/940)... For trisyllabic words, final stress is still prominent (64%, 790/1,235)"; quadri-/pentasyllables mostly stress S2; "Kaxabu defaults to a final stress pattern... if the initial syllable contains a long vowel or diphthong, it carries primary stress. Additionally, affixations like patient voice and imperative can cause stress to shift."
sources.locator: p.248 (literature summary), Table 8 p.258, p.260, Conclusion p.264

sources.citation: Macaulay, Benjamin. 2020. The prosodic structure of Pazeh. In Ileana Paul (ed.), Proceedings of the Twenty-Sixth Meeting of the Austronesian Formal Linguistics Association (AFLA 26), 175ff. London, ON: University of Western Ontario.
sources.quote: "The last syllable in the IP is always prominent"; "Blust (1999, 332) provides an alternative: stress is underlyingly on the last syllable of the stem, and if suffixes are added, a 'stress shift' rule moves stress to the ultima."; "All IP's in Pazeh have stress on the final syllable. In some cases, stress/tonal alignment fall both on the final syllable and on an additional syllable... Non-final stress always occurs on long vowels, /ai/, and /au/." Kaxabu (after Lim 2016): "stress is rhythmic, with iambs built from the end of the prosodic word."
sources.locator: sec. 2.1 (p.176-177) and sec. 2.2 'Prominence on Non-Final Syllables'; sec. 3.1 on Kaxabu

sources.citation: Macaulay, Benjamin. 2019. The Prosodic Structure of Pazeh. AFLA 26 abstract, University of Western Ontario.
sources.quote: "Previous descriptions mention only final stress, and penultimate lengthening [Ferrell 1970; Blust 1999]." "Stress always falls on the last syllable of the IP... IP's may have a non-final stress in addition to final stress. These fall on syllables containing long vowels, or the sequences /ai/ /au/."
